h1:
Songkhla–Phatthalung 3 Days
Circling the Lagoon Between Two Provinces
intro: Songkhla and Phatthalung share the same body of water — Songkhla Lake, the largest brackish lagoon in Thailand. Most visitors fly into Hat Yai and only see the Songkhla side, yet driving up the western shoreline to Phatthalung is perfectly doable in a single day. This 3-day plan stitches both provinces together: start in Songkhla's Sino-Portuguese old town and Samila Beach, cross to Koh Yo via the Tinsulanon Bridge on day two, then on day three hug the lake shore north into Phatthalung, ending at Thale Noi wetland and Pak Pra Canal where giant bamboo fish traps and wild water buffalo make for an entirely different Thailand. Timings and stops are laid out so you won't drive in circles or miss the highlights people routinely pass by.
chips: 🎨 Songkhla Old Town — Nang Ngam Road
🦬 Thale Noi — Pak Pra Giant Fish Traps

blocks.html: The best way to do this trip is fly into Hat Yai, rent a car, and drive yourself — public transport simply doesn't reach most of the key spots along the lake. From Songkhla town up to Thale Noi in Phatthalung is about 100–110 km and takes roughly 1.5–2 hours depending on your route. Day 1 covers Songkhla old town and Samila Beach. Day 2 loops through Koh Yo and the lakeside temples. Day 3 heads north to Phatthalung for Thale Noi and Pak Pra Canal before looping back.

blocks.title: Know Your Route Before You Go
blocks.html: Songkhla Lake has two sides. Taking the western shore (Phatthalung–Khao Chai Son–Pak Phayun) gives you glimpses of the lake at regular intervals and is the more direct line to Thale Noi. The main Highway 4083 runs along the peninsula side through Sathing Phra and Ranot — useful if you want to cross the Chaloem Phrakiat 80th Anniversary Bridge (Ranot–Khuan Khanun), a 5+ km causeway spanning the lake, but it adds time. Decide before you leave.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Songkhla Old Town — Nang Ngam Road, Street Art & Samila Beach

items.activity: Walk the old town: Nang Ngam, Nakhon Nok & Nakhon Nai roads
items.note: The three-street old quarter is packed with century-old Sino-Portuguese shophouses and street murals that tell everyday Songkhla life. Go on a weekday morning — crowds are thin and the light is soft before the heat kicks in.

items.activity: Old-school snacks: clay-pot ice cream and Pa Mol's charcoal egg cake
items.note: Nang Ngam Road is the real food street here. The fresh-coconut clay-pot ice cream is the signature snack; Pa Mol's charcoal-grilled egg cakes with butter filling always has a queue. Graze as you browse the shophouses.

items.activity: Lunch at Keat Fang stew rice
items.note: Keat Fang is an old-town institution serving Songkhla-style pork and ox-tongue stew over rice — the kind of dish you won't find easily elsewhere. It's been going long enough to become a local landmark. Expect a crowd at noon.

items.activity: Café break in a heritage building — EP's Cafe or similar
items.note: The neighbourhood has several cafés tucked into old shophouses. EP's Cafe on Nang Ngam Road is popular. Sit out the worst of the afternoon heat here before heading to the beach.

items.activity: Samila Beach — Golden Mermaid statue and the Cat & Mouse rocks
items.note: Samila is Songkhla's iconic town beach. The Golden Mermaid statue is the province's symbol; nearby, the Cat and Mouse rock formations sit just offshore near Koh Nu (Mouse Island) and Koh Maeo (Cat Island). Good for a breezy stroll.

items.activity: Sunset + seafood dinner by the beach
items.note: The late-afternoon light is good for silhouette shots of the mermaid. The stretch from Samila to Chalatat has plenty of seafood restaurants facing the sea. Sleep in Songkhla town tonight.

blocks.title: Stay in Songkhla Town or Hat Yai?
blocks.html: If the priority is strolling the old town and chilling by the sea, staying in Songkhla town is the most convenient — you can walk out early before the crowds arrive. If you want more dining, shopping, and nightlife options, Hat Yai is about 30 km away; drive in for the day and return in the evening. Pick whichever fits your style.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Koh Yo → Tinsulanon Bridge → Wat Laem Pho

items.activity: Khao Tang Kuan & Khao Noi — city views from the hilltops
items.note: Before leaving town, climb Khao Tang Kuan for a panorama that takes in Samila Beach and Songkhla Lake in a single frame. There's a chedi and relics at the summit; a lift operates during opening hours.

items.activity: Cross the Tinsulanon Bridge to Koh Yo
items.note: The Tinsulanon Bridge is the longest bridge crossing Songkhla Lake — it connects the mainland to Koh Yo in two spans. Driving across, the lake opens up on both sides. There are pullover spots at the approaches for photos.

items.activity: Wat Laem Pho — large reclining Buddha
items.note: This old temple on Koh Yo has a large reclining Buddha (Phra Norn) with the Tinsulanon Bridge and the lake as a backdrop. Free entry; dress modestly.

items.activity: Lunch: fresh sea bass from the lake cages
items.note: Koh Yo is known for sea bass farmed in floating cages in the middle of the lake. The waterfront restaurants serve it steamed, fried, or in soup — genuinely fresh, priced fairly at source.

items.activity: Institute of Southern Thai Studies + Koh Yo woven fabric
items.note: The Institute of Southern Thai Studies is a small museum covering Southern Thai culture and daily life; entry is around THB 50–100. Koh Yo is also known for its traditional woven fabric in the Rachawat pattern, and local shops sell seaweed salad, shrimp paste, and dried fish as souvenirs.

items.activity: Head back to town — stop at the Songkhla National Museum
items.note: On the way back, the Songkhla National Museum occupies a fine old Chinese-style building in the city centre and covers the province's history and the peninsula. Closed Monday–Tuesday; check the schedule.

items.activity: Dinner in town + second night in Songkhla
items.note: Rest up tonight. Tomorrow is the longest drive of the trip — up to Phatthalung and Thale Noi.

blocks.title: Timing on Koh Yo
blocks.html: The island's main draw is the fresh sea bass — lakeside restaurants tend to be busiest from noon to mid-afternoon, and later in the day some places run out of fish or fill up fast. The ideal approach is to cross the bridge mid-morning and have lunch on the island, then visit the Institute of Southern Thai Studies in the early afternoon when the heat starts to ease.

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Lake Road North into Phatthalung → Thale Noi → Pak Pra Canal

items.activity: Check out and drive north to Phatthalung along the lake
items.note: About 100–110 km from Songkhla town, roughly 1.5–2 hours. The route through Khao Chai Son gives intermittent lake views; the landscape shifts from coast to paddy fields and limestone hills as you enter Phatthalung.

items.activity: Thale Noi — longboat ride through the wetlands
items.note: Thale Noi is a large wildlife sanctuary and Ramsar wetland site, home to hundreds of species of waterbirds. A chartered longboat tour runs about 1–1.5 hours; hiring a whole boat costs around THB 400–600 and can take several passengers. The red lotus blooms are at their best from late February through May.

items.activity: Watch the water buffalo herd wading in the wetland
items.note: Thale Noi has a herd of water buffalo that wades out into the water to graze on aquatic plants — a sight you won't find many other places in Thailand. The boat operator will bring you close to where the buffalo typically enter the water. Early morning and late afternoon are when they come out most.

items.activity: Lunch: khao yam and Southern Thai dishes near Khuan Khanun
items.note: Phatthalung does a very good khao yam (herbal rice salad) and bold Southern curries. The area around Khuan Khanun and Pak Pra has local spots and waterside eateries. Try the khao yam with a Southern curry before moving on.

items.activity: Pak Pra Canal — the giant fish traps (yor yak)
items.note: Pak Pra Canal feeds into Songkhla Lake and is famous for its rows of giant bamboo lift-net traps (yor yak) standing in the water. It's one of Phatthalung's most-photographed scenes — most striking at dawn or in the angled late-afternoon light.

items.activity: Drive back to Hat Yai / airport
items.note: From Pak Pra it's about 100–120 km back to Hat Yai, roughly 2 hours. Allow extra time for car return and airport check-in. If you have time to spare, a roadside café in the rice fields or a Phatthalung souvenir market works well as a final stop.

blocks.title: Go to Thale Noi Early
blocks.html: Thale Noi and Pak Pra Canal are at their best in the early morning — calm water, soft light, more birds, and the buffalo out in numbers. If you actually want the sunrise-over-the-fish-traps shot, consider sleeping one night in Phatthalung and taking a dawn boat. If you're doing it as a day trip from Songkhla, leave early enough to arrive at Thale Noi before mid-morning.

blocks.text: Rough Budget per Person (3 Days, 2 Nights)

items: 2 nights' accommodation — mid-range options in Songkhla / Hat Yai from around THB 1,000–2,000; split between two people
6–7 meals — roughly THB 800–1,500 depending on how much seafood and Koh Yo sea bass you order
Thale Noi boat charter — around THB 400–600 for the whole boat; split by headcount
Institute of Southern Thai Studies / museum entry — around THB 50–100 per venue
Car rental + fuel — a compact car runs around THB 900–1,400/day; fuel for the full trip around THB 800–1,200/car, split between passengers
A comfortable mid-range total comes to roughly THB 2,500–4,000/person (the more people sharing the car, the better the deal)

blocks.text: Can You Do This Without a Car?

blocks.html: You can, but you'll miss the freedom of cruising along the lake shore. In Songkhla, songthaews, motorbike taxis, and Grab cover the main town; the old town and Samila Beach are walkable from each other. Koh Yo and the Tinsulanon Bridge require a charter or a rented motorbike. Thale Noi in Phatthalung has no direct public transport to the site — the practical options are a train or minivan from Hat Yai to Phatthalung town, then a chartered songthaew or motorbike taxi out to the wetland. If you'd rather not piece that together, a private car with a driver hired by the day makes much more sense when there are a few of you splitting the cost.

blocks.title: Best Time to Visit
blocks.html: The southern Gulf coast gets heavy rain during November–December — the lake can be choppy and Thale Noi boats may not run. The comfortable window for clear skies is February–May, which also coincides with the red lotus bloom at Thale Noi. The giant fish traps at Pak Pra and the water buffalo herds look best in that period too. Midday sun is intense year-round, so bring a hat and water.

faq.q: Is 3 days enough to cover both Songkhla and Phatthalung?
faq.a: Comfortably, if you have a rental car. Day 1 takes care of Songkhla old town and Samila Beach; Day 2 crosses to Koh Yo via the Tinsulanon Bridge and visits Wat Laem Pho; Day 3 drives the lake shore north to Thale Noi and Pak Pra Canal and back. If you want to be at Thale Noi at dawn, add a night in Phatthalung.

faq.q: How long is the drive from Songkhla to Thale Noi in Phatthalung?
faq.a: About 100–110 km, which takes roughly 1.5–2 hours depending on your route. Going via Khao Chai Son is the most direct and offers lake views along the way. If you want to cross the Chaloem Phrakiat 80th Anniversary Bridge over the lake (the long causeway near Ranot), you'll take the peninsula side and need to allow more time.

faq.q: When is the best time to see the water buffalo and red lotus at Thale Noi?
faq.a: The water buffalo wade out to graze mainly in early morning and late afternoon. The red lotus blooms are at peak from late February through May. For both at once in good light, take an early morning boat — charter rates are around THB 400–600 for the whole boat, shared between passengers.

faq.q: Do you need to take a boat to reach Koh Yo?
faq.a: No — Koh Yo sits in the middle of Songkhla Lake but the Tinsulanon Bridge connects it to the mainland by road. Just drive across. On the island you'll find Wat Laem Pho, the Institute of Southern Thai Studies, lakeside sea bass restaurants, and shops selling Koh Yo woven fabric and seaweed salad. Half a day covers it comfortably.

faq.q: What is the best month to visit Songkhla and Phatthalung?
faq.a: February through May is the sweet spot — clear skies, and it's also when the red lotus blooms at Thale Noi. The giant fish traps at Pak Pra and the water buffalo look great in that period. November and December bring heavy rain to this part of the south; the lake can be rough and Thale Noi boats may cancel. Check the weather before booking.
